\item The \emph{static} traits, which describe values denoted by
expressions composed from literals, operators (described in
\secref{constant-values}), and \KWD{bool}, \KWD{nat},
and \KWD{int} parameters; here the type
does not encode the value of the expression, but the value of the
expression can nevertheless be known statically if specific
values are specified for the static parameters.  Also, in situations
where the type of an expression composed solely from literals and
operators nevertheless cannot be described by a constant trait, then a
static trait may be used to describe it instead.
For example, a static expression \EXP{2(3+m)} where \VAR{m} is a
\KWD{nat} parameter has trait \TYP{NaturalStatic}.
\end{enumerate}

\Library\ declare none of the constant traits.
An expression composed only of numerals and operators is folded, before the
static check and on both implementations, into a \emph{signed constant}, which
holds its value exactly and whose kind its operands give: computed from
numerals without a radix point and without a quotient, it is an integer,
written as an integer numeral or a negated one; computed from numerals without
a radix point with a quotient among its operations, it is a quotient, written as
the reduced quotient of two integer numerals; and computed from a numeral with a
radix point, it is written as a numeral with a radix point, or a negated one,
where its denominator divides a power of ten, and otherwise as the reduced
quotient of two numerals whose numerator has a radix point.
Where nothing fixes the type of a signed constant (\secref{literals}), an
integer takes the default of an integer numeral, a quotient the type
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and a constant computed from a numeral with a radix point the
type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, whatever its value, so that \EXP{6/3} is a
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{0.5 + 0.5} an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}; where a place fixes
a type, the constant is converted into it as a numeral is, with at most one
rounding.
So \EXP{2147483647 + 1} is the \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} \EXP{2147483648},
\EXP{-2147483648} is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{x = 7/2} binds the
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} \EXP{7/2}, and \EXP{0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3} is \VAR{true}.
The operators whose result depends on the width of a type, the wrapping and
saturating operators, the bitwise operators and the shifts, are not folded, nor
is a division by zero, nor an operation whose floating-point result could be a
negative zero: their operands take their types, and the operator its meaning
there.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 gave a constant
expression a constant trait whose static arguments encode its value, as
\EXP{\TYP{IntegerConstant}\llbracket\VAR{false}, 3+5\rrbracket}, and no library
declares those traits.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that an expression of numerals alone is
folded exactly into a signed constant, which takes one of three defaults where
nothing fixes its type: the value that a constant trait would encode in its
static arguments is held in the constant itself, written as numerals, so that a
coercion of a program's own sees only the four numbers of a numeral as written
(\secref{literals}).}


The only operation on literals that produces a new literal (as opposed
to a constant) is concatenation by using the operator \EXP{\|}.
One may concatenate mixed string and
character literals, producing a string literal.
For example, ``\txt{foo}''\EXP{\|}''\txt{bar}'' yields ``\txt{foobar}''.
One may also concatenate two natural numerals
of the same radix, producing a new natural numeral of that radix.
For example, \EXP{\mathtt{deadc}_{16} \| \mathtt{0de}_{16}} yields \EXP{\mathtt{deadc0de}_{16}}.
\revision{revival-string-literals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 states
the concatenation of string literals, which neither of the team's
implementations built.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that a concatenation of two string
literals, as of a string and a character literal, is folded into one string
literal before the static check, on both implementations, and so denotes one
object (\secref{literals}).}
\revision{revival-numerals}{The concatenation of two natural numerals of the
same radix is built as written: before the static check, on both
implementations, it is folded into one natural numeral, whose digits are the
digits of both numerals in order, leading zeros among them, so that its four
numbers (\secref{literals}) count them.}

Every literal trait extends an appropriate constant trait, and every
constant trait extends an appropriate static trait.  So every
literal is also a constant expression, and every constant expression
is a static expression.

convenient to be able to use an integer-valued expression
in a floating-point expression even though its
type is not a subtype of any floating-point type.  Fortress supports
the automatic conversion of values of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and of integer
numerals, to the floating-point type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (the technical term for this kind of automatic
conversion is coercion); a value of any other integer type is converted to
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} explicitly (\secref{basic-rationals}).  In
this way one can write \EXP{(x + 1)/2} rather than \EXP{(x +
1.0)/2.0}, for example.  Such coercion applies generally to function
and method (collectively called as functional) calls as well as to
operators; one can write \EXP{\ln 2} rather than \EXP{\ln 2.0}, or
\EXP{\arctan(1,1)} rather than \EXP{\arctan(1.0,1.0)}, for example.
\revision{revival-int-float}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
Fortress supports the automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point
values.
The revival decided on 26~September 2026 that a conversion between number
types is a coercion where it is exact and stays explicit where it can lose
precision, and \library\ declare the coercion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} from
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and the decision names the integer numerals too.
The conversion from \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, though exact, stays explicit, since
that decision names only \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and the numerals.
The examples of this paragraph convert numerals and are unchanged.
\Library\ give an integer numeral the type \TYP{NaturalNumeral}, from which
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} coerces with one rounding; the compiled type checker,
against \library, and the interpreter convert an integer numeral where
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} is declared, whatever its value (\secref{literals},
\secref{revival-numerals}).
The compiled path's own library declares no coercion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
from an integer type or an integer numeral; there \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and integer
numerals convert to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} only explicitly, and the other integer types not at all.}

One way to think about coercion is that if type \VAR{T} can be coerced
to type \VAR{U}, then a value of type \VAR{T} can be used to ``stand
in'' for a value of type \VAR{U} in a functional call, for example.  This is
different from actually \emph{being} of type \VAR{U}; it means only
that, given any value of type \VAR{T}, an appropriate value of type
\VAR{U} can be computed to substitute for it.  Also, coercion occurs
only when the declared type of the corresponding parameter in the
functional declaration is exactly the type \VAR{U} being coerced to

 \VAR{T} can be coerced to type \VAR{U} then any subtype of \VAR{T}
 can also be coerced to type \VAR{U}.

A numeral's conversion into its default (\secref{literals}) is not a coercion,
and applies where coercion does not: where the declared type is a supertype of
the default, as \TYP{Any}, \TYP{Object} and \TYP{Number} are, or is a type
parameter declared without a bound, and where no type is declared.
At a call, a numeral is applicable without coercion to a parameter of its
default type and to a parameter of a type that fixes no type for it; its
conversion into any other type is a coercion
(\secref{applicability-with-coercion}).
So of the declarations \EXP{h(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)} and
\EXP{h(x\COLON\TYP{Any})}, both applicable to \EXP{h(5)} without coercion, the
call invokes the first, which is the more specific.
A numeral at a type of a program's own that declares no coercion from the
numeral's type is not converted into its default and then coerced, since
coercion does not chain (below); it is a static error.

whose declared type is a supertype of the type converted to.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that a numeral where nothing fixes a
type is converted into its default; the default is a rule beside coercion, and
the paragraph above stands as it was.}

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
number types, and where nothing at its place fixes a type it is converted into
its default (\secref{literals}): a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value does not fit in the narrower type, and an
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} for a numeral with a radix point.
Nothing fixes a type at a variable declared without a type; at a parameter of
type \TYP{Any}, \TYP{Object} or \TYP{Number}, or of a type parameter declared
without a bound; at the receiver of a dotted method call whose method the
default type declares; and at a static argument that only numerals fix.
A type parameter that several numerals fix, and no other argument and no
expected type, is instantiated at the narrowest default that holds every one of
their values, an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} where any of them has a radix point, each
numeral being converted into it exactly: so for
\EXP{\VAR{pick}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(a\COLON{}T, b\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T}, the call
\EXP{\VAR{pick}(3, 3000000000)} is instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and the
list \EXP{\langle 3000000000, 0.5\rangle} is a
\EXP{\TYP{List}\llbracket\mathbb{R}64\rrbracket}.
The branches of an \KWD{if} or \KWD{case} expression whose value is bound to a
variable declared without a type are read in the same way: numerals there take
the narrowest default that holds them all.
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
its default: a numeral without a radix point as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value does not fit in the
narrower type, and a numeral with a radix point, whose conversions into
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} tie, as an
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values; and \EXP{\VAR{round}(2.50000000000000001)}, whose numeral the
declarations of \VAR{round} on \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} would leave tied, rounds the \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} nearest to
that numeral, and is 2.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The revival's text of 28~September 2026 read a
numeral at its default only where its conversions tie, and only a numeral
without a radix point.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that a numeral takes its default at
every place that fixes no type, that a type parameter that several numerals fix
takes the narrowest default that holds them all, and that a numeral with a
radix point whose conversions tie is read as an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.}

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{StaticParam} &::=& \KWD{nat} \emph{Id} \\

Static parameters may include one or more
\KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters.
Syntactically, a \KWD{nat} parameter consists of
\KWD{nat} followed by an identifier.
An \KWD{int} parameter consists of
\KWD{int} followed by an identifier.
These parameters are instantiated at runtime with numeric values.
A \KWD{nat} parameter may be used to instantiate other
\KWD{nat} parameters, or to appear in any context that a
variable of type \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can appear,
except that it cannot be assigned to.
An \KWD{int} parameter may be used to instantiate other
\KWD{int} parameters, or to appear in any context that a
variable of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} can appear,
except that it cannot be assigned to.

content.content:
31:The Draft says nothing of fields or getters on a numeral, and nothing of when a program's coercion runs. Its one use of the numeral types outside this passage is the binary chapter's coercion with `where` clauses over static parameters (`advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1661`), which he declined to fulfil at 23:02.
90:- 23:02 (L4982): "our coerce is a novel design, not this one. I basically said it will be a call. To initializer that must consume the fields from the numerals." He said this about the binary chapter's `where` arithmetic, which he declined to fulfil. His clarification on 11-09: he was explaining his understanding that the specification gives a custom type a way to read the original literal from the source by implementing the coercion; the coercion is not a run-time method call; it is the interface a custom numeric type implements, where the compiler has a chance to hand it the parameters from the source code.

content.content:
## 4. What it is not

- Not a `Numeral` value object with getters for the four numbers, `asFloat`, `asString` and `=` pairs with the number types.
- Not a coercion called at run time on such an object.
- Not the compiler prelude's `IntLiteral` or `FloatLiteral`.
- Not walk building a numeral object at a site's first evaluation and calling the coercion on it.

## 5. His words that carry each point

- 12:36 (L3260), on float numerals: "whatever ends up in QQ doesn't lose this precision. Whenever we know that we are saving the literal into float with fixed size, we should do the relevant conversion with maximum precision."
- 20:11 (L4329): "float literal is basically a QQ with implicit coercions to all other numerics. ... How could we get the promise of the conversion? Like, maybe we should try it on our own numeric types. What if we tried it with complex numbers? ... how would we try to stress test this concept of literal during a conversion like this so that we arrive at the right shape?"
- 20:18 (L4350): "didn't you just quote the solution from the specification with Radix point numeral? Like, I am seeing this for the first time here. Isn't the solution to implement this? I haven't seen it in walk, and we haven't seen it in compile path."
- 20:23 (L4361): "the specification was saying that you go for the conversion, that this conversion happens at compile time. We would never instantiate so many types at runtime, right? It is a compile time type. It doesn't exist at runtime."
- 20:29 (L4423): "the specification promises that the radix point numeral is a compile time conversion. It can only live on the right side of an assignment or declaration, and the left side must be a different type. You will never get radix point numeral or natural numeral at runtime."
- 21:22 (L4640): "We have the literals defined using this radix type. Like, we finished the design as the specification says. Does that solve all of our problems here? Do we need to prototype something to make this running?"
- 21:34 (L4676): "You never write int literal and float literal with the generic parameters N, M, R, and V. ... Value is the last of these generic parameters. It's the V at the end. ... how would you access those numbers inside the float literal? ... show me the code. ... use the same example that they use, those intervals. Show me the old way and the new way."
- 21:38 (L4689): "why can't we change the nat to be ZZ? Like a arbitrary precision integer, basically a big int. We are putting it into the type, so it must have a fixed size so that we can stamp the class. Is that the reason?"
- 21:40 (L4700): "this thing is supposed to be a compile time thing only. ... these are not runtime things. Why can't we accept for these types in a checker arbitrary precision size for the value?"
- 21:55 (L4749): "NAT, N-A-T, is just a natural number in generic type system with no limits. We have, for practical purposes, implemented it for the compile path as something that is ZZ32 ... But NAT is just a number that can be used in compilers' computations. ... Why can't we build it the specifications way? Just finish the original design. Why not? This way there is no runtime type that you are calling methods on that is not the compile time way, right? Using just the type system declaration for the coercion seems more elegant to me. The original drafts way."
- 22:02 (L4813): "how do I convert a numeral, a constant written in the program's name, into an instance of a custom numeric type? And you do it by letting the parser give you the four numbers, and you put them into the object's during compile time to compute its fields, so that you can stamp that object as a compile time constant."
- 22:14 (L4823): "you are saying the compiler runs coerce only at runtime. It is not what the specification says. We have just prototype constant folding. Isn't this a specific instance of constant folding? Because I see it as one. What am I missing?"
- 22:19 (L4833): "I disagree that coerce is running of arbitrary code. Coerce is just invocation of the numeric type constructor that gets the constants from the parser. That's all. It is just instantiation of the numeric types constructor using the values from the generic parameters of that coerce method. Invokes only constructor of the numeric type using the constants it has on hand. Like the type must provide a constructor that gets those parameters. That's it. That's the coercion."
- 22:21 (L4846): "That's what I had in my head. Does this match, can this be reconciled with what's written in the specification?"
- 22:33 (L4878): "Why do you keep talking about in literal and float literal when I said I will take the drafts originals? These two names, int literal and float literal, are from compiled library and from the glue classes in the walk interpreter. None of these were mentioned in the original specification, which defined the type for the natural numeral, radix numeral. We are going with those."
- 22:40 (L4903): "We'll go with machine defaults. When the type is not declared."
- 23:02 (L4982): "our coerce is a novel design, not this one. I basically said it will be a call. To initializer that must consume the fields from the numerals." He said this about the binary chapter's `where` arithmetic, which he declined to fulfil. His clarification on 11-09: he was explaining his understanding that the specification gives a custom type a way to read the original literal from the source by implementing the coercion; the coercion is not a run-time method call; it is the interface a custom numeric type implements, where the compiler has a chance to hand it the parameters from the source code.
- 23:10 (L5019): "Doesn't the natural numeral imply there is no sign, that it's only positive numbers, or am I mixing things up?"
- 11-09 13:20 (L6379): "I never gave up working draft static parameter form. Where do you get this?" 13:22 (L6388): "No fucking getters. Where wasn't I clear enough? I was talking about constant folding."

## 6. What he accepted from the coordinator

- The `static final` at class load as the JVM's nearest form of a stamped object constant: point 3 of the coordinator's list at 22:20 (L4838), "the compiler emits a call of it with the four numbers as constants, once per class, into a `static final` field. The type's code builds the object from the four exact numbers. No double in between, no literal object alive in the program, no class per numeral." His "That's what I had in my head" (22:21) answered that list. The paragraph after the list, "a `coerce` takes one parameter, so the four numbers travel as one value with four fields", was labelled "The only Fortress detail left is spelling"; his word of 11-09 is that he never gave up the static parameters.
- The machine defaults where nothing fixes a type: his own choice (22:40), after weighing the restart's `QQ` and `ZZ` (22:31, L4856) against microGPT's untyped hyperparameters and `asZZ32` on every index (22:32, L4874).
- The six repairs and the defaults of the Fable judgement, at 23:23 (L5096), "Yeah. Option one." The form, static parameters or fields, was not among them; it was already written as settled.

## 7. Where the design turned

- 21:56 (L4752): the coordinator asked the prototype worker to cost the Draft's way "by reading only, no build". 22:00 (L4809): the report back, "The Draft's static-parameter way needs a size kind beyond 32 bits, typed constants in the class loader, a new `where` form for `v < 256`, and walk's half after walk runs the checker; none of that is sized, and all of it is large." Four minutes. Nothing built. Recommendation: "B with the hybrid".
- 22:20 (L4838): "You're right, and that settles it." Four points, then the fields paragraph as "spelling", and "The Draft's static-parameter form is the same call with the numbers as static arguments, at the cost of a class per numeral and a wider `nat`, which buys nothing here."
- 22:22 (L4849): "your design puts them into the numeral's value as fields". 22:33 (L4881): "the four numbers are fields of the numeral's value, not static parameters of its type." 22:46 (L4971): "With the four numbers as fields, as you decided".
- 22:41 (L4911; commit `e9e03d6fe4`): the held list, under "His decision on literals": "carrying the Draft's four numbers ... as fields of the numeral's value, not as static parameters".
- 23:04 (L4987): the Fable judge's brief, headed "The decision, in the curator's words and the coordinator's condensation": "as fields of the numeral's value, not as static parameters of its type"; "the compiler emits that call once per class, at load, with the numbers as constants."
- 23:35 (L5159): the compaction summary that handed the Fable session to the Opus one: "carrying the four numbers n, m, r, v as fields, replacing IntLiteral and FloatLiteral"; "A program's coercion is emitted as a call with constants, once per class at load, into a static final field."
- 23:52 (commit `69427e9422`): P-174, by the Opus record writer: "they are fields of the value, not static parameters of the type"; "which the compiler calls once per class, when the class loads". His one quoted sentence stops before "using the values from the generic parameters of that coerce method".
- 11-09 00:5x: the Fable review of the batch record weighed "the Working Draft's static parameters" as "against P-174's 'fields of the value'; not a way for this batch" (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-29-review.md:69`).
- 11-09 13:18 (L6345): the Fable fidelity reviewer, "he said this while arguing for the Draft's static-parameter form, which he then gave up"; 13:19 (L6349) the coordinator's relay, "read through the four getters".

## 8. What was built against it

From the fidelity review (`explorations/reviews/numeral-fidelity-2026-11-09.md`, sections 1 and 2) and the recheck (`scratchpad/numeral-fidelity/recheck.md`, sections 1.4 and 2.8):

- The one library: `trait Numeral extends Number comprises { NaturalNumeral, RadixPointNumeral }` with four abstract getters, `digits`, `fractionDigits`, `radix`, `digitValue`; `value object NaturalNumeral(digits: ZZ32, radix: ZZ32, digitValue: ZZ)` and `value object RadixPointNumeral(digits: ZZ32, fractionDigits: ZZ32, radix: ZZ32, digitValue: ZZ)`, each with `getter asString()`, `asFloat(self): RR64` and eleven `=` pairs each way with the number types (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:454-494`). No static parameters.
- Walk: a numeral runs as its default value with the four numbers attached; at a program's own type walk builds the library's numeral object at run time, one per site, and calls the program's `coerce` with it at the site's first evaluation, not at load; the body reads `x.digitValue` or calls `asFloat(x)` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java:292-337`; test `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralOwnTypeWalk.fss`).
- The compiled path: numerals at built-in types fold at compile time with one rounding. At a program's own type the program still writes `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` or `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)` against the prelude, whose values give `asZZ32` to `asRR64`, not the four numbers; the class's static initializer calls it once per site; at a generic program type it runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957).
- A negative constant reaches a program's coercion signed on both paths: under walk `t: Tally = -3` passes `NaturalNumeral(1, 10, -3)`, whose `asString` prints `7` (rows 961, 968; review-queue item 448), against repair 3, "a program's coercion sees the four numbers of a written numeral only".
- The fidelity review's verdict, "carried out faithfully in their substance", checked the build against P-174 and the held list, and P-174 carries the coordinator's framing.

So of section 3: points 1, 2 at a program's type, 3 and 4 are not built; point 2 at built-in types, point 5 and point 6's fold are built; point 7 is met in part (the compiled path at a program's type waits for the switch-over); point 8's tests exist only as the review's probes and the prototype's three cases.

## 9. Open questions for the design discussion

Questions, not answers:

1. The fold that batch 29 landed makes `-3` one signed constant before the checker. Under the design a numeral has no sign. How does `-3` reach a program's coercion: as the type's own unary minus applied to the coercion of `3` (repair 3), and what does a type without a unary minus do? Where in the library's algebraic traits is unary minus declared, and how does that bear on it?
2. Walk has no checker. How does walk hand the four numbers to a generic coercion and run it once per site, with no numeral object? Today walk refuses a `nat` parameter used as a value (row 486), and walk does not convert through a generic coercion (row 513).
3. The checker's static arithmetic is 32-bit today (`nat` as `NN32`, F-67). What does `v` of a 20-digit numeral need in the checker, and in the class loader's stamped constants (F-129)? Is a class name's text enough, as the coordinator said at 21:38?
4. Can the checker evaluate a `where { v < 256 }` on such a coercion, so that a byte type refuses `300` at compile time? What part of the static-expression system, marked "not yet supported" (`constant.tex:14`), does that need?
5. The library's own number types through the same coercions: does the fold of a library coercion give the same constant and the same speed as today's direct fold? Which of the library's eight types declare a coercion from each numeral type, and in which form?
6. The `=` pairs between a numeral and a number type, kept at 23:23 as a default: are they needed at all when every numeral converts at compile time? What does `5 = n` for `n: NN32` become?
7. A bare numeral's printing: the team's `NumberPrintTest.fss:16` prints a 32-digit numeral as written. Under the design a bare numeral defaults to `RR64` and prints 16 digits. Is that the bend he takes?
8. microGPT's lines: `(epsilon, lr0, beta1, beta2, epsilon_A, nSteps) = (10.0^(-5), 0.01, 0.85, 0.99, 10.0^(-8), 1000)` and the others with untyped numerals. What does each become under the design, and does any bit change?
9. The compiled path before the switch-over: nothing may be added to the compiler's prelude (P-37), so a program's own type cannot write `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)` compiled until the switch-over. Does the design wait for the switch-over there, or is an exception to P-37 taken?
10. A numeral type written anywhere but a coercion's or an operator's parameter: refused by the checker (P-174's clause), and what walk does.

## 10. The probe he wants next

One Opus worker, at extra high effort, builds the static-parameter form for real, in a worktree seeded from the batch 29 landing, on both paths: the numeral types with the four numbers as static parameters in the checker, the fold of a program's generic coercion into one constant per site (a `static final` at class load on the compiled path; walk's equivalent), and the library's own number types through the same mechanism. Its tests are his own types, written first and seen failing: complex from `3 + 4 i`, the Draft's interval, `Dec(unscaled, scale)` from `3.14159`, bfloat16 rounding once from the exact value, the round trip printing `C.8_16` back from the four constants, a byte type refusing `300` at compile time, and `0.1_2 SEQV 0.5` true with `0.1 = 0.1_16` false. It measures what each part costs in lines, in the checker's time and in the count and distance stages, what it does to the library's types' speed, and which tests flip. It reports what it could not build and why, as decisions not taken. Reading-only costing is not accepted: the Draft's way was costed by reading in four minutes on 11-08, and that is where the design turned.

\subsection{The conversion into a float, declared by each number type}
\seclabel{revival-asfloat}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{basic-rationals}; \secref{revival-numbers}.
\item[Change] The passage on the conversions between number types says that
the explicit conversion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x)}, is the
method that each number type declares, and that \TYP{Number} itself declares
no conversion, where it said that \library\ declare the method on
\TYP{Number}.
The change of \secref{revival-numbers} says the same.
\item[Rationale] The revival decided on 6~November 2026 that \VAR{asFloat}, and
the \EXP{=} that the library built on it, leave the trait \TYP{Number}, and that
each of the library's number types keeps its own \VAR{asFloat}.
The team's later compiler library declares \TYP{Number} with nothing in it
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss}, lines
510--511, in the revival's repository), and declares its conversion into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} on each of its number types, not on a shared trait; the
Working Draft names no such method.
With \TYP{Number} open to a program's own number types, an abstract
\VAR{asFloat} would oblige a program's complex number to give a float, and an
\EXP{=} on \TYP{Number} built on it would call two different complex numbers
equal.
\Library\ now declare \VAR{asFloat} on \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and the two numeral types
\TYP{NaturalNumeral} and \TYP{RadixPointNumeral} (\secref{revival-numerals};
\nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi};
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi}), and the vector
norm at each of the eight number types as its element type.
A reversal would declare \VAR{asFloat} on \TYP{Number} again, abstract, with an
\EXP{=} built on it, so that every type below \TYP{Number} must give a float, or
declare it on a new trait that the number types extend.
\item[Effect] \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x)} is unchanged at every number type of the
library.
Two numbers of different types compare by \EXP{=} where a coercion carries one
into the other: for each of the library's fourteen coercions between number
types, and each of its eleven from the two numeral types
(\secref{revival-numerals}), the type converted to declares \EXP{=} at the type
converted from, and that type declares \EXP{=} at the first, each converting
the narrower operand as the coercion does.
Two numbers of different types that no coercion joins, as a \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}
and an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, compare by the library's fallback \EXP{=} over
\TYP{Any}, which answers \EXP{a \sequiv b}; a program that means their values
writes the conversion, \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x) = y}.
Two values of different types are never strictly equivalent
(\secref{equivalence}), so that fallback answers \VAR{false} for them, on the
interpreter as in the compiled code's helper.
A number type of a program's own compares by the \EXP{=} it declares, or else by
the fallback.
\item[Original text] The Working Draft of February 2011 has no such sentence:
the revival added it in its own text of 27~September 2026, not the Working
Draft's.
The passage said, in \nolinkurl{Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex}, lines
46--49, before this revision:
\begin{quote}
Every other conversion between number types is written explicitly;
in particular, a conversion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} from
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, or \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}
is explicit, written \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x)} with the method that \library\ declare on \TYP{Number}.

and the change of \secref{revival-numbers} said that the conversion into

\TYP{Number}''.

\subsection{The type of an integer numeral}
\seclabel{revival-numeral-type}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{literals}; \secref{coercion}.
\item[Change] \secref{literals} says that \library\ give every numeral without a
radix point the type \TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the
number types, and that each of the five integer types, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a coercion from it.
The box of \secref{coercion} says the same of the coercion into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, and that the interpreter does not yet give a numeral that
type.
The change of \secref{revival-numerals}, of 8~November 2026, replaced this
text: an integer numeral has the type \TYP{NaturalNumeral}, beside
\TYP{RadixPointNumeral} for a numeral with a radix point, and is converted into
its default where nothing fixes a type; this entry keeps the change of
29~September 2026, and its effect below states what of it holds since then.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 29~September 2026 that a numeral has a type of its own, \TYP{IntLiteral},
from which each number type converts, the compiled path's own library's working
version taken in place of the numeral types of \secref{literals}, which no
library declares, and that \library\ take it before the interpreter does, since
the interpreter can give a numeral that type without changing the declarations
its calls reach only once it runs with the static types of the compiled type
checker.
\Library\ declared their numeral type an object extending \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
its arithmetic withheld by the comment ``Do not enable these until coercion is
implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals.''
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss}, lines
495--496 before this change, in the revival's repository).
Coercion is implemented on both paths now, and \library\ declare the type as
the compiled path's own library does
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi}, lines
390--431): beside the number types under \TYP{Number}, with the arithmetic that
comment withheld, each integer type declaring a coercion from it.
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, which that library does not declare from
a numeral, coerce from it too, since \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} coerces from every integer
type (\secref{basic-rationals}) and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} from integer numerals
(\secref{revival-int-float}).
\item[Effect] The type \TYP{IntLiteral} of this change is named
\TYP{NaturalNumeral} in \library\ since the change of \secref{revival-numerals};
the compiled path's own library keeps the name \TYP{IntLiteral}.
The compiled type checker converts an integer numeral to the
integer type, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} or \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} that its context expects,
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} among them, which refused a numeral
before.
A numeral beside a value of an integer type is converted to that type where no
declaration of the operator is applicable to the two without coercion, and that
type's own declaration of the operator is then the most specific
(\secref{resolving-coercion}); \library\ state on each integer type the
comparisons \EXP{<}, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{>} and \EXP{\geq}, \OPR{CMP},
\OPR{MAXNUM}, \OPR{MINNUM} and a power with a numeral exponent, which the types
inherited before from a declaration that a converted numeral leaves tied with
those of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
Equality is stated in pairs instead: each integer type declares an \EXP{=}
whose parameter is of type \TYP{NaturalNumeral}, and \TYP{NaturalNumeral} one whose
parameter is of each integer type, and each converts the numeral by its
coercion into the integer type and compares by that type's own \EXP{=}
(\secref{basic-rationals} gives the pairs of the other number types).
Inequality is not stated in pairs: the top-level declaration of \EXP{\neq},
whose parameters are of type \TYP{Any}, is applicable to an integer value and a
numeral without coercion, and since the change of \secref{revival-numerals} it
receives the numeral at its default, which it compares with the integer value by
\EXP{=}; so \EXP{u \neq 0} is \VAR{true} for a zero \VAR{u} of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}
or \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, neither of which declares \EXP{=} with
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, as the interpreter answered before, a departure from
\secref{operator-NE} that the effect of \secref{revival-numerals} names.
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} states in its api, for the same reason, the additive and
multiplicative operators its body declares.
\TYP{IntLiteral} declared its own \VAR{zero}, \VAR{one}, \VAR{even},
\VAR{odd}, \VAR{floor}, \VAR{ceiling}, \VAR{truncate}, \OPR{DIVIDES},
\OPR{TIMES} and a power with a numeral exponent; \TYP{NaturalNumeral} declares
none of them, since an expression of numerals alone is folded and a numeral
reaches those of its default type (\secref{revival-numerals}).
A numeral given where any integer type is accepted, as the count of a shift,
is converted to the narrowest of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} that holds its value, as \secref{numeral-default} reads a
numeral whose conversions tie.
The interpreter converts an integer numeral where its place fixes a type, and
gives it its default elsewhere (\secref{revival-numerals}).
Its calls of the comparisons, \OPR{CMP}, \OPR{MAXNUM} and \OPR{MINNUM} on an
integer type reach that type's own declarations, which answer as the

with a converted argument, which stopped at a tie with those of
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} or answered at \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, now answer at the integer
type both arguments convert to.

\Library\ define coercions

\subsection{The inference of a call's static arguments}
\seclabel{revival-inference}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \chapref{type-inference}; \secref{ranges};
\secref{basic-integers}; \secref{revival-ranges}; \secref{revival-notrevised}.
\item[Change] \chapref{type-inference}, which held a heading and two draft
notes, states how the static arguments of a call that does not write them are
inferred, for type parameters and for \KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters.
The declaration is chosen first, as \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses it, a
declaration with static parameters being applicable to a call if some instance
of it within its bounds is, and compared on the parameter types it declares.
Its static arguments are then inferred: a type, \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
parameter that a parameter type mentions inside another type is fixed by the
argument, and a type parameter that the return type mentions inside another
type by the expected type; a type parameter that
is the whole type of parameters takes the narrowest type that their arguments
are substitutable for, which for number arguments is the narrowest type into
which every one of them converts, and otherwise, since 29~September 2026, its
bound (below); every
argument is admitted by substitutability, the coercions the instance needs are
inserted statically, and the converted call dispatches by subtyping.
A call written by tight juxtaposition, as a method invocation or as an operator
application, has an expected type in the contexts the chapter lists, a variable
or field declaration and an assignment to a variable among them, and is
inferred again without it when its result then converts.
A numeral whose conversions tie is read as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} by its value; any other tie among
declarations applicable only with coercion is a static error.
On 8~November 2026 the rule for numerals widened (\secref{revival-numerals}):
a numeral takes that default at every place that fixes no type, a type
parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds them
all, and a numeral with a radix point is read as an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
The chapter lists what it does not yet describe, the static arguments of a
\KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator parameter among them, keeps the
second of the two draft notes, and has three boxes: on the Working Draft, the
bound it assumes and the passages it leaves to the revision of the overloading
chapters; on the interpreter; and on a type parameter that only the return
type mentions and on the \KWD{bool} parameters that neither implementation
infers.
The ranges section says that a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
component converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an integer numeral does, with a
box.
The box in \secref{basic-integers} says that a generic call over two different
integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into by the rule of
\chapref{type-inference}.
\secref{revival-notrevised} says that the rule is written and names the passages
the chapter leaves unrevised, and it and the effect of \secref{revival-ranges}
say that the question of a \KWD{nat} parameter in a range is settled.
On 29~September 2026 one sentence of the rule changed.
Of a type parameter that is the whole type of parameters, where no narrowest
candidate exists and the rule for numerals does not settle the tie, the
chapter said that it ``takes the union of the types of those arguments
(\secref{internal-types}), if its bounds permit that, and none of those
arguments is converted''; it now takes the intersection of its upper bounds,
its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none, and what the expected type
requires of the declared return type, none of those arguments converted, with
a box.
With the revision of the overloading chapters (\secref{revival-overloading}),
the first box points to this entry's list of the cases in which the compiled
type checker departs from the chapter and no longer names the passages that revision revised, and the box
on the interpreter says to which type the interpreter binds such a type

\subsection{Which objects are value objects}
\seclabel{revival-object-kinds}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] The opening section of \chapref{objects}, its list of
the kinds of objects.
\item[Change] Its sentence on the value objects named booleans, numeric
literals, IEEE floating-point numbers and integers; it now names integers of
every precision and rational numbers too.
Its sentence on the reference objects named arbitrary-precision numbers and
aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets; it now names strings and the
aggregates.
The passage gains one box.
The rule of strict equivalence (\secref{equivalence}) is unchanged: values of
different types are never strictly equivalent, value objects of one type are
when their fields are, a binary word by its bit pattern, and reference objects
only when they are one object.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows two
decisions of the revival.
By the first, of 6~November 2026, the values of the arbitrary-precision integer
and rational types are value objects: \library\ declare the arbitrary-precision
integer as a value object, and the sentence's own list called integers value
objects and arbitrary-precision numbers reference objects, so the text
disagreed with itself and with the library; the library's declaration is the
deliberate word.
By the second, of 6 and 7~November 2026, strictly equivalent means the rule of
\secref{equivalence} on both implementations, with no special case for any type,
and strings are reference objects: \library\ declare every kind of string as an
object without the \KWD{value} modifier, so two strings are strictly equivalent
only when they are one object, and their text equality is their own \EXP{=}.
The Working Draft of February 2011 named no kind for strings, and the
team's implementations compared two flat strings by their text and two ropes
by identity.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md}, section~2.4, and
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/string-equivalence-2026-11-06.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] Both implementations answer \EXP{\sequiv} by the rule, and both
read the \KWD{value} modifier.
\Library\ declare the rational type's object and the two numeral types,
\TYP{NaturalNumeral} and \TYP{RadixPointNumeral}, as value objects.
A numeral is converted where it stands on both implementations
(\secref{revival-numerals}), so a floating-point numeral bound to a variable of
type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} is strictly equivalent to a computed \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
value of the same bits, and \EXP{x \sequiv z} is \VAR{true} for \EXP{x = 3} and
\EXP{z\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = 3} on both.
Two string literals of one text are one object (\secref{revival-string-literals}),
so \EXP{\hbox{\rm``\STR{ab}''} \sequiv \hbox{\rm``\STR{ab}''}} is \VAR{true}, and
a string built as a program runs is not strictly equivalent to an equal literal
unless the operation that builds it answers an existing string.
The departures:
the compiled path's own library, used until the one library replaces it,
answers \EXP{\sequiv} on values of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64},
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, on strings and on booleans by

reaches the rule, so there two equal strings built apart are strictly

and \library\ declare \EXP{=} on pairs and triples only, so two tuples of four
or more elements are equal only when they are strictly equivalent, and two such
tuples of equal strings built apart are not equal (row~923 of the revival's
gap ledger).
The answers are gated by \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk.fss},
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/ValueObjectCC64Walk.fss} and, for the compiled
helper, by \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleCompiled.fss}.

content.content:
\secref{object-traits}.
Objects contain \emph{methods} (described in \secref{methods}) and
\emph{fields} (described in \secref{fields}).

An object is a \emph{value object}, a \emph{reference object},
or a \emph{function object}:
It is a function object if it has an arrow type,
a reference object if it has an object trait type
that is not declared with the \KWD{value} modifier
(see \secref{value-objects}),
and a value object otherwise
(i.e., if it has a tuple type, the type (),
or an object trait type declared
with the \KWD{value} modifier).

A value object cannot have mutable fields,
and it is completely determined by its type,
environment and its fields:
Value objects with the same type, environment and fields
are indistinguishable.
Thus, an implementation may freely copy value objects.
Most objects with simple standard types,
such as booleans,
numeric literals,
IEEE floating-point numbers,
integers of every precision,
and rational numbers are value objects.
%
In contrast,
reference objects are thought to ``reside in memory'',
and are identified by an \emph{object reference}.
A new object reference is created
whenever a reference object is constructed,
so that reference objects constructed separately are always distinct.
What about reference objects that have no mutable fields?
Reference objects include
strings
and aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets.
\revision{revival-object-kinds}{The Working Draft of February 2011 named
arbitrary-precision numbers among the reference objects and gave strings no
kind.
The revival decided on 6~November 2026 that the values of the
arbitrary-precision integer and rational types are value objects, as \library\
declare them, and on 6 and 7~November 2026 that strings are reference objects:
two strings are strictly equivalent only when they are one object, and their
text equality is their \EXP{=}.}
Two string literals of the same text denote one object, so that a string
literal evaluated twice, and two literals of one text, are strictly equivalent;
a string that a program builds as it runs is another object than a literal of
the same text, unless the operation that builds it answers an existing string
(\secref{literals}).
\revision{revival-string-literals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 did not
say whether a string literal denotes one object.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that two string literals of one text are
one object, on both implementations; strings remain reference objects.}

\subsection{Integers in floating-point expressions}
\seclabel{revival-int-float}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{coercion}.
\item[Change] The automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point values
becomes that of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} values and of integer numerals to
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64}; any other integer type converts to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
explicitly.

\subsection{A native binding that names a static helper}
\seclabel{revival-native-helpers}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{FortressBuiltin}: the comment of
\VAR{builtinPrimitive} in the \apiN\ \TYP{FortressBuiltin}, which this
specification typesets from the \apiN's source file.
\item[Change] The comment says that the argument of \VAR{builtinPrimitive}
names either a glue class, a subclass of
\texttt{com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.NativeApp}, which only the
interpreter runs, or a helper, a public static method of a Java class of the
package \texttt{com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers}, which both the interpreter
and the compiled code call; that the interpreter loads a helper beside its glue
classes, taking among the methods of that name the one whose Java parameter and
result types carry the declared types, \KWD{self} first, and carrying each value
at its declared type; that the compiler, before type checking, rewrites such a
body into a call of the helper, which the type checker checks against the
helper's Java signature; and that a string under that package that names no
such method is an error on both.
It also names the package that defines the subclasses of the classes
\texttt{NativeFn0} to \texttt{NativeFn4}
\texttt{com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim}, where it said
\texttt{com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.primitive}, a package that the
implementation does not have.
The comment gains a box.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
revival's decision of 10~October 2026 that every native binding of \library\
keeps the library's own form, a body that is exactly a call of
\VAR{builtinPrimitive}, and that its string names a static helper of the
package \texttt{com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers}, the compiled code's own
helpers, in place of a glue class, which takes the interpreter's values and
which the compiled code cannot call.
The bindings move onto helpers step by step, and the type checker checks each
moved binding against its helper's Java signature from the step that moves it.
The alternative not taken was \KWD{import} \KWD{java} declarations written in
the source files of \library, the compiler's own form for its natives, which
the interpreter does not run.
A reversal would restore the original comment, put the moved bindings back on
their glue classes, and leave the compiled code without a binding of the
natives of \library\ that it can call.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-natives-walk/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The specification's revision

POSITIONS.md:120
- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** When the revival changes the language, it updates `Specification/` with the change, so that the text and the implementation do not disagree. The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). Every such change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). The unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, is never touched. Why: an open disagreement between the text and the implementation would confuse a reader.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:41
- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.

FACTS.md:43
- F-46 **Route C, the patents' forest rule with a return-type rule over every level of a chain, closes the specialisation hole (F-45), but going back to a nested number tower under it needs work beyond the checker.** The library's tower was nested before route A flattened it (P-43). Built as a shadow checker on 2026-09-24 and run through the zero probe's stack on a library copy without the reduction markers, route C refuses 25 pairs at 21 of the nested tower's declarations: specialisations that a level below does not cover. Completing the tower needs seven more declarations and the identification of `Integral[\ZZ32\]` with `ZZ32`. The patents' `comprises T` on the self-typed traits licenses that identification, but it overflows the checker's stack (measured on the zero probe's copy of the checker, in the recursion of `Formula.scala` that the tree shares). A hierarchy check of its own could enforce the identification instead; none is built. Leaving route A for route C also needs: the tower nested again; the call-site fix in every dispatcher (F-136); in the code generator, a method for each middle level of a chain, whose absence, by the error text, makes such a chain die with `AbstractMethodError`; walk to accept the specialised pairs without overflowing on `comprises T`; and, for the identification, a way past the checker's overflow or the hierarchy check. The decided design (P-173, P-174, P-76, P-172, P-171, P-165, P-40) is written into the specification in the revision form (P-96), with two new Appendix I entries and four revised. content.content:
# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild

**tree**
: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.

**library order**
: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.

**DSL grammar**
: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.

**parser directory**
: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.

## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:

- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.

## Two layers of code

The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.

The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.

The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:

- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.

An edit makes stale what was built from it:

- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.
